one_liner: Single-file C coroutine runtime with Go-like channels, deterministic scheduler and epoll/kqueue I/O; about 11 ns switches, no baseline measured.
what_it_does: Neco gives a C program single-threaded concurrency in the style of goroutines: neco_start(fn, argc, ...) spawns a stackful coroutine, and the library supplies sleep/yield/suspend/resume/join, channels, generators, mutexes, condition variables, waitgroups, deadlines and cancellation. POSIX-style wrappers (neco_read, neco_write, neco_accept, neco_dial, neco_getaddrinfo) block only the calling coroutine by parking it on an epoll (Linux) or kqueue (macOS/BSD) event queue. It is a different interface from pthreads or any C++ std facility, not a drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: Context switches go through the bundled llco layer, a hand-written assembly register swap (callee-saved registers only, no signal-mask syscall) adapted from minicoro and Lua Coco. Scheduling is done by the bundled sco, a fair FIFO scheduler, entirely in user space. Stacks are 8 MiB mmap regions grouped with 1 MiB gaps, recycled via a stack free list and with early page release, and coroutine and channel objects are pooled; blocking writes on Linux and getaddrinfo are pushed to worker threads so the scheduler thread keeps running.
when_to_use: Network servers or clients in plain C on Linux/macOS/FreeBSD where you want sequential code per connection instead of callback state machines (the author's Bluebox Redis clone is the reference design).
Programs with thousands to tens of thousands of mostly idle coroutines on one core.
Simulations or tests that need deterministic, reproducible interleaving (fair, deterministic scheduler).
Projects that want a single .c/.h drop-in under MIT with no external dependencies.
when_not_to_use: CPU-bound work that should scale across cores: one scheduler per thread, cross-thread communication only via pipes/eventfd/atomics; multithreaded scheduling is an explicit non-goal.
Windows or WebAssembly network code: neco_wait and fd-based I/O are not available there (no epoll/kqueue), Windows is amd64 only, and guards, CSPRNG and unwinding are missing.

Code that must call blocking libraries using pthread_mutex_t/pthread_cond_t from inside coroutines (README: they do not work well), or that must coexist with another event loop such as libuv (issue #5 open).

Bursty spawning of many coroutines: neco_start switches into the new coroutine immediately, and issues #10 (slow creation of thousands of coroutines) and #12 (about 105,050 switches for 100 spawns among 1,000 coroutines) report the cost.

integration.dependencies: none beyond libc and pthreads (dlsym used for getaddrinfo threads); epoll or kqueue for I/O
integration.min_toolchain: C11 with <stdatomic.h> (GCC or Clang); glibc 2.30+ reported for Linux (issue #6)
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, FreeBSD full; Windows amd64 and WebAssembly (Emscripten -sASYNCIFY) core coroutines only
integration.thread_safety: One runtime and scheduler per thread; neco objects are not shared across threads; pthread mutex/cond are unsuitable inside coroutines

gotchas: Coroutine argv pointers are valid only until the coroutine's first neco_* call; copy arguments first (README example 4).
Default stack is 8 MiB of virtual memory per coroutine plus 1 MiB gaps (1 MiB heap stacks on Windows/WebAssembly); guard pages need -DNECO_USEGUARDS.
neco_start called first from main() blocks until that coroutine and all children finish; neco_main changes program behavior slightly (see API docs).
Signal handling and worker threads are on by default on POSIX; disable with NECO_NOSIGNALS / NECO_NOWORKERS when embedding in a host that owns signals or threads.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Neco over libdill or libmill when you want a maintained, single-file C runtime with channels, deadlines and networking wrappers plus deterministic scheduling; pick llco or minicoro when you only need the switch primitive, and libdill when you want published switch numbers against a baseline (Go goroutines).
verified_claims_summary: The README states that an llco-based context switch takes about 11 ns on the author's AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, with no compiler, flags, benchmark code or comparison library. The linked Bluebox repo (not part of the verified claim) shows memtier_benchmark default runs on the same CPU at 493,346 ops/s for the Neco-based Redis clone versus 207,735 ops/s for redis-server (about 2.4x, derived from page data), an application benchmark against a far larger server, not a coroutine comparison.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-05-30), MIT, 1.4k stars, single 8,761-line neco.c with a test suite claiming 100% coverage under sanitizers and Valgrind; six issues open, including C++ export, Windows sockets and old-glibc support.
